title: Bhagwa Dhwaj vs Tricolour: India's Independence Day Celebrations Hit by BJP-Congress Flag Wars
excerpt: As BJP launches its fourth Har Ghar Tiranga campaign, opposition leaders question why the RSS took 52 years to hoist the national flag at its Nagpur headquarters.
body:
• BJP's nationwide Tiranga Yatra runs August 10-14 ahead of Independence Day, this year also celebrating Operation Sindoor. Opposition parties call it political theatrics.
  • Karnataka Home Minister Priyank Kharge has demanded that the RSS register, disclose finances, and pay taxes — challenging the organisation in its centenary year.
  • The Karnataka government's order regulating private organisations on public property was stayed by the High Court, but the political battle over the flag continues.

India's 79th Independence Day celebrations on August 15 have become a political arena, with the ruling BJP's annual Har Ghar Tiranga campaign drawing sharp pushback from opposition parties who accuse the Sangh Parivar of appropriating the Tricolour while historically favoring the saffron Bhagwa Dhwaj.

The BJP launched a nationwide Tiranga Yatra running from August 10 to 14, its fourth consecutive year of the Har Ghar Tiranga campaign. This year's edition doubles as a celebration of Operation Sindoor, the Indian military strikes launched in May against terrorist targets across the border. Senior leaders including Sambit Patra, Vinod Tawde, and Tarun Chugh are coordinating the campaign across regions.

52 Years Without the Tricolour

The sharpest attacks have come from Karnataka Home Minister Priyank Kharge, who has turned the flag question into a running confrontation with the RSS.

https://x.com/PriyankKharge/status/2087736452428046397

"Every time anyone questions the RSS, the BJP loses its composure. An organisation that made no contribution to the freedom struggle now lectures the nation on patriotism — and it took 52 years for the Tricolour to be raised at their Nagpur headquarters."

— Priyank Kharge, Karnataka Home Minister

Kharge's reference is to a well-documented fact: the RSS headquarters in Nagpur did not hoist the Indian national flag for over five decades after independence. The organisation's historical preference for the Bhagwa Dhwaj — the saffron flag — over the Tricolour has been a recurring point of political attack, one that gains fresh salience every August.

In Karnataka, the issue has moved beyond rhetoric. The state's Congress-led government approved an order in October 2025 requiring private organisations to seek prior government approval before using public property for events — a measure widely understood as targeting RSS route marches and shakhas on government grounds. The Karnataka High Court stayed the order weeks later, but the political confrontation has only intensified.

RSS at 100: Registration Row Escalates

In June 2026, Kharge escalated the dispute with a public letter to RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, demanding that the organisation register formally, disclose its finances, and pay taxes. He cited the RSS's own internal report claiming 4,127 daily shakhas, 1,389 weekly milans, and 562 route marches with over two lakh uniformed participants in Karnataka alone.

"If citizens, labour unions, NGOs, trusts, temples and companies are expected to register, disclose and comply with the law, why should the RSS remain exempt?" Kharge wrote.

The RSS, celebrating its centenary year, maintains that it operates as an unregistered "body of individuals" — a classification it says has been recognised by courts and the Income Tax Department. Bhagwat is scheduled to meet young people in Nagpur on Independence Day as part of an outreach initiative focused on youth participation.

Opposition Calls Yatras 'Theatrics'

The NCP (Sharad Pawar faction) joined the criticism, calling BJP's Tiranga Yatras "theatrics" and questioning the sincerity of an organisation that champions the national flag while its ideological parent historically shunned it.

The criticism echoes similar attacks from previous years. Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav has previously accused the BJP of pursuing "selfishness in the name of nationalism" and alleged that the party's flag campaigns have led to distribution of incorrectly printed tricolours and forced participation in schools and offices.

In Karnataka, the flag row has a specific local trigger: the Keragodu incident, where Congress leaders accused BJP supporters of placing the Bhagwa Dhwaj on a flagpole designated for the national flag. Chief Minister Siddaramaiah said at the time that it was "not right to hoist the Bhagwa dhwaja instead of hoisting the flag of India."

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

Independence Day is among the most widely observed national events in the Indian diaspora. From flag hoistings at Indian consulates to community gatherings across the United States, August 15 is a unifying moment for NRIs of every political stripe.

The politicisation of the Tricolour — and the question of which organisations genuinely championed it — resonates differently abroad, where the flag often represents cultural identity rather than partisan affiliation. For diaspora Indians watching from a distance, the annual Bhagwa-Tiranga argument is a reminder that even the most unifying national symbols carry contested political histories at home.
nri_angle: Independence Day is one of the most widely celebrated events for NRIs, making the political fight over the Tricolour directly relevant to diaspora Indians who observe August 15 as a cultural and national identity marker.
